summary:
TerraAnalog is a full-stack web application and companion notebook workflow that discovers and evaluates Earth environments as quantitative planetary analogs for candidate Moon and Mars exploration sites. Rather than relying on visual lookalikes or only well-known testbeds, TerraAnalog’s Express backend queries live NASA POWER climatology, Open-Meteo (Copernicus/SRTM) 5×5 terrain elevation grids, NASA CMR granule catalogs (NISAR, MODIS LST, SMAP), NASA EONET v3 hazard streams, and NASA PDS Geosciences ODE archives (LRO, MRO, MGS) alongside cited planetary mission baselines.
Users can compare 12 curated sites—including underexplored evaporite basins, impact craters, and hydrothermal salt domes—or click anywhere on an interactive NASA GIBS map to probe arbitrary coordinates in real time. A client-side engine standardizes six physical axes (mean temperature, thermal swing, aridity/cryo-ice, slope and roughness, aeolian dust, and solar flux) via Z-scores and user-tunable weights, rendering radar and seasonal comparisons, PDS browse imagery, and EONET correlations.
By pairing every similarity score with explicit physical breakdown limits—such as gravity, vacuum or thin CO₂ pressure, and regolith chemistry—TerraAnalog enables transparent, reproducible analog selection to guide instrument testing and mission planning for future lunar and Mars exploration.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

TerraAnalog is a full-stack web application and companion research workflow for discovering, ranking, and auditing terrestrial planetary analog sites against Moon and Mars exploration targets using open NASA and geospatial data.

  • Live Terrestrial & Planetary Data Aggregation (server.ts): An Express backend (with a 30-minute in-memory TTL cache and AbortController request timeouts) fetches live Earth telemetry for 12 curated terrestrial sites—spanning classic testbeds (Devon Island, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Kverkfjöll, Teide), our companion notebook AOIs (Salamat/Chad Basin, Atacama Yungay), and underexplored candidates (Qaidam Basin yardangs, Dallol hydrothermal salt domes, Richat Dome, Chott el Djerid, Salar de Uyuni, Aouelloul Crater)—plus any arbitrary global coordinate probed by the user:
    • NASA POWER Climatology: Retrieves 8 meteorological/radiative parameters (T2M, T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN, PRECTOTCORR, ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN, WS10M, RH2M, CLOUD_AMT).
    • Copernicus / SRTM Local Terrain (via Open-Meteo Elevation): Samples a 5×5 coordinate grid (0.02° spacing) around each site to compute mean elevation, latitude-corrected 3×3 central finite-difference slope (°), RMS roughness (m), and relief (m).
    • NASA Earthdata CMR & EONET v3: Queries live granule counts (NISAR_L2_GCOV_PROVISIONAL_V1, MOD11A1, SPL3SMP_E), nearby hazard counts, and regional/global natural events.
    • NASA PDS Geosciences ODE REST: Queries live orbital product counts (results=c) and sample footprints/browse JPEGs (results=cmf) across 7 Moon and Mars reference targets (LRO Diviner/LOLA/LROC and MRO/MGS HiRISE/CTX/MOLA/SHARAD), paired with published mission literature baselines.
    • OSM Nominatim: Reverse-geocodes user-clicked coordinates into country, region, and place names.
    1. Global Matrix: Interactive NASA GIBS Blue Marble Leaflet map with click-to-probe anywhere on Earth, weight sliders, 6-axis interactive SVG radar chart, 12-month climatology vs. planetary mean chart, ranked CSV export, and strength/breakdown cards.
    2. GIBS & EONET: Multi-date NASA GIBS WMTS tile viewer (MODIS Terra/Aqua TrueColor, VIIRS NOAA-20, MODIS Terra Daytime LST) with EONET event overlays, category bars, CSV export, and a 6×6 Pearson correlation matrix.
    3. PDS Moon & Mars: Instrument coverage matrix and live PDS ODE query inspector displaying real orbital browse imagery and archive links.
    4. Methodology: Documents the equations, datasets, software stack, and scientific limits.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Replaces subjective visual comparison with physics-based scoring: Two deserts can look similar in true-color imagery while differing sharply in thermal swing, moisture/ice activity, terrain roughness, and solar flux.
  • Mission-tunable prioritization: Engineers and scientists can adjust dimension weights in real time (e.g., emphasizing terrain slope/roughness for rover mobility trials or aridity/temperature for cryogenic drill/astrobiology studies).
  • Global search beyond overused sites: Users are not limited to a static catalog—they can click anywhere on the map or enter coordinates to immediately evaluate unstudied locations with live telemetry.
  • Built-in orbital data readiness: Automatically reports how many NISAR, MODIS LST, SMAP, and PDS (HiRISE, LOLA, Diviner, SHARAD) products already cover each terrestrial AOI and planetary target.
  • Exportable outputs: One-click CSV downloads for both ranked analog tables and filtered EONET event records.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Broaden analog field site discovery: Surface overlooked terrestrial environments (such as high-altitude evaporite yardang basins, polar impact structures, or small fresh sandstone craters) that offer distinct physical testing advantages for Artemis lunar operations and future Mars missions.
  • Make analog selection transparent and reproducible: Every score can be traced back to live NASA/DEM measurements, explicit weighting equations, and cited planetary baselines.
  • Prevent over-claiming in analog science: By placing "Where the Analogy Breaks Down" directly beside every similarity score, TerraAnalog encourages honest test design—highlighting where Earth gravity (1.0 g), atmosphere (101.3 kPa), rain weathering, or lack of perchlorates/agglutinates limit how far a terrestrial test extrapolates.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Coding Languages: TypeScript (^7.0.2), TSX/JSX, HTML5, CSS3, and Python (in the two companion .ipynb research notebooks in public/assets/aistudio/).
    • Frontend: React 19, Vite 8, Tailwind CSS v4 (@tailwindcss/vite), Leaflet 1.9.4 (streaming EPSG:3857 NASA GIBS WMTS tiles), custom SVG charting components, lucide-react, and IBM Plex Sans/Mono fonts.
    • Backend: Node.js (v22), Express 4.21.2, and tsx (^4.21.0).
  • Open APIs & Datasets: NASA POWER Climatology API, NASA Earthdata CMR (granules.json), NASA GIBS WMTS, NASA EONET v3, NASA PDS Geosciences ODE REST (oderest.rsl.wustl.edu/live2), Open-Meteo Elevation API (Copernicus/SRTM DEM), and OpenStreetMap Nominatim.
  • Companion Python Notebook Stack (public/assets/aistudio/*.ipynb): earthaccess, requests, numpy, pandas, scipy, xarray, h5netcdf, netCDF4, h5py, rasterio, rioxarray, geopandas, shapely, pyproj, scikit-learn (StandardScaler, euclidean_distances, RandomForestClassifier, KMeans), torch/torchvision, ultralytics (YOLO11n random-weight contract), opencv-python-headless, scikit-image, matplotlib, seaborn, folium, plotly, and optional pds.peppi.
  • Hardware / Runtime Environment: Developed and hosted in a standard Linux cloud web environment (Node.js container / Cloud Run via AI Studio Build) accessed via standard web browsers; the companion Python notebooks were structured for Google Colab (with optional GPU support for vision/PyTorch experiments). No specialized field or custom hardware was built.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Interactive "Any-Point-on-Earth" Laboratory: Rather than limiting users to pre-saved locations, clicking any point on Earth dynamically constructs a 25-point 5×5 DEM lattice, calculates local finite-difference slope and RMS roughness on the fly, pulls multi-decade NASA POWER climatology and orbital archive counts, reverse-geocodes the region, and ranks it instantly against Moon and Mars targets.
  • Built-In Scientific Self-Critique: Instead of presenting a naive single "percent match," every comparison displays per-dimension match breakdowns alongside specific physical warnings (e.g., high precipitation chemical weathering, excessive temperature gaps, lunar vacuum vs. Earth wind).
  • Unified Multi-Agency Open-Data Bridge: Connects terrestrial climate, local topography, Earth hazard streams, SAR/optical granule catalogs, and off-world PDS orbital imagery inside one cohesive console without requiring authentication tokens from the user.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Strict Domain Separation: Earth-specific EONET hazard taxonomies (wildfires, floods, storms, sea/lake ice) and Web Mercator Earth projections are strictly quarantined from Moon and Mars PDS archives so terrestrial phenomena are never misapplied to other worlds.
  • Zero-Fabrication & Provenance Clarity: We avoided synthetic data generation—keeping runtime generative AI completely out of the data pipeline (@google/genai is unused in runtime code), separating live API telemetry from cited planetary literature baselines (PLANETARY_SEEDS), and auditing every missing-value/fallback path (such as NASA POWER -999 sentinel filtering and null coalescing in analogEngine.ts).
  • Real-World API Constraints & Resilience: To prevent timeouts and truncated counts (for example, PDS ODE capping results=cmf counts at 100 and requiring explicit pt= product-type codes), we split exact count queries (results=c) from sample browse queries (results=cmf), batched elevation and PDS calls, added strict timeouts, and implemented 30-minute caching.
  • Spatial & Physical Limitations: We explicitly accounted for scale differences between coarse gridded climate/elevation data (~2.2 km 5×5 lattice) and high-resolution orbital imagery (25 cm/px HiRISE), as well as irreducible planetary differences in gravity, atmospheric pressure, radiation, and regolith chemistry.
